random-variable-parameters-s1.title: Tacos per order at a food truck
random-variable-parameters-s1.text: A food truck tracks how many tacos each order contains. Let X = the number of tacos in a randomly chosen order (invented data).

table.caption: Probability distribution of X, tacos per order

random-variable-parameters-s2.title: A fundraiser game
random-variable-parameters-s2.text: A school fundraiser game costs \$2 to play. A player wins \$10 with probability 0.10 and \$5 with probability 0.15, and otherwise wins nothing. Let W = a player's net gain in dollars (prize minus the \$2 cost) on one play.

table.caption: Probability distribution of W, net gain on one play

items.q: What is the mean (expected value) of X?

options: That averages 1 to 5 without the probabilities.
That is the most likely value, not the mean.
Right: each value weighted by its probability.
That averages the probabilities, which always gives 1 divided by the number of values.
3 tacos
2 tacos
2.5 tacos
0.2 tacos

items.q: What is the standard deviation of X, to two decimal places?

options: That is the variance. Take its square root.
That treats 1 to 5 as a data set with no probabilities.
That is the squared deviation of 2 or 3 from the mean, not the whole sum.
Right: the square root of the weighted squared deviations, 1.25.
1.25 tacos
1.58 tacos
0.25 tacos
1.12 tacos

items.q: Which is the best interpretation of the mean of X in context?

why.correct: An expected value is a long-run average: over many randomly chosen orders, the average number of tacos per order is about 2.5.
options: Right: a long-run average over many orders.
No order contains 2.5 tacos; the most common is 2.
That would describe a median; here 55% of orders have fewer than 2.5.
The mean does not predict one order; it describes the long run.
Over many orders, the average number of tacos per order is about 2.5
Most orders contain 2.5 tacos, the most common order size
Half of the orders have more than 2.5 tacos and half have fewer
The next order will contain about 2 or 3 tacos

items.q: Write the expression for the expected value of W.

mistakes.why: That averages the three values as if they were equally likely. Weight each value by its probability.
The \$2 loss happens with probability 0.75 and must be included: add (−2)(0.75).
Those are the prizes, not the net gains. W subtracts the \$2 cost: use 8, 3 and −2.

items.q: What is the standard deviation of W, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the variance. Take the square root.
That treats 8, 3 and −2 as a data set. Use the probabilities as weights and the mean, −0.25.

items.q: The expected value of W is −\$0.25. Build an interpretation in context.

why.correct: An expected value is a long-run average. A negative mean net gain means players lose money on average, which is how the school raises money.

claim.label: Meaning
options: If many people play, players lose an average of about \$0.25 per play
Each player loses exactly \$0.25 every time the game is played
A typical player wins \$0.25 on most plays

why.1: On any one play a player gains \$8 or \$3 or loses \$2; the \$0.25 is an average over many plays.
why.2: The mean is negative, and 75% of plays lose \$2.

evidence.label: So
options: so the school raises about \$0.25 per play in the long run
so the game is fair to the players
so the school loses money on the game

why.1: A fair game would have an expected net gain of 0.
why.2: Players lose on average, so the school gains on average.

conclude.model: If many people play the game, players lose an average of about \$0.25 per play, so in the long run the school raises about 25 cents for each play.

items.q: The school expects 400 plays at the fair. About how much money should the game raise?

why.correct: The mean net gain for a player is −\$0.25, so the school gains about \$0.25 per play on average: $400 \times 0.25 = 100$ dollars. The actual total will vary by chance.
options: Right: 400 plays times an average of \$0.25 to the school.
That is the \$2 cost times 400, ignoring the prizes paid out.
That counts only the \$3 net from small prizes; the prizes reduce what the school keeps.
That is 0.25 times 100 plays, not 400.
About \$100
About \$800
About \$1,200
About \$25

items.q: Which is the formula for the mean (expected value) of a discrete random variable X?

why.correct: Weight each value by its probability and add: $\mu_X = \sum x_i p_i$.
options: That is the mean of a data list with no probabilities.
Right: the probability-weighted average of the values.
The probabilities alone add to 1.
That has the shape of a standard deviation.
$\mu_X = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}$
$\mu_X = \sum x_i p_i$
$\mu_X = \sum p_i$
$\mu_X = \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 p_i}$

items.q: Let D = the number of defective bulbs in a randomly chosen box of 4, with $P(D = 0) = 0.70$, $P(D = 1) = 0.20$, $P(D = 2) = 0.08$ and $P(D = 3) = 0.02$. Find the expected value of D.

mistakes.why: That averages 0, 1, 2 and 3 without the probabilities.
That averages the probabilities. Multiply each value by its probability and add.

items.q: Let D = the number of defective bulbs in a randomly chosen box of 4, with $P(D = 0) = 0.70$, $P(D = 1) = 0.20$, $P(D = 2) = 0.08$ and $P(D = 3) = 0.02$. The mean is 0.42. Find the standard deviation of D.

mistakes.why: That is the variance. Take the square root for the standard deviation.

items.q: Random variables P and Q both have mean 3. P takes the values 2, 3 and 4; Q takes the values 0, 3 and 6. Each has probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25 for its three values. Which has the larger standard deviation?

why.correct: Q's values lie farther from the mean (3 away) than P's (1 away), with the same probabilities, so Q varies more: $\sigma_Q = \sqrt{9(0.5)} \approx 2.12$ and $\sigma_P = \sqrt{1(0.5)} \approx 0.71$.
options: Right: larger deviations from the mean, same weights.
Values closer together mean less spread, so a smaller SD.
Equal probabilities with different distances give different spreads.
The same mean says nothing about spread.
Q, because its values lie farther from the mean of 3
P, because its values are closer together
They are equal, because the probabilities are the same
They are equal, because the means are both 3

items.q: For the tacos distribution, $\sigma_X \approx 1.12$. What does this mean in context?

why.correct: The standard deviation of a random variable is the typical distance of its values from the mean, in the long run.
options: A standard deviation is a distance in tacos, not a percent of orders.
Right: a typical distance from the mean, in tacos.
Orders come in whole tacos, and the SD measures spread on both sides.
The mean is exact for this distribution; the SD describes how orders vary.
About 1.12% of orders differ from the mean of 2.5 tacos
The number of tacos in an order typically varies by about 1.12 from the mean of 2.5
Most orders contain between 2.5 and 3.62 tacos
The mean of 2.5 tacos per order could be off from the truth by about 1.12 tacos

items.q: For a randomly chosen family in a town, the expected number of children is 1.8. A student says this is impossible, since no family has 1.8 children. How should you respond?

why.correct: An expected value is a long-run average over many families. It need not be one of the possible values.
options: Rounding throws away information; the average is 1.8.
Means of counts are often not whole numbers.
Right: the long-run mean can fall between whole numbers.
The mean alone does not say what most families have.
The student is right: it should be rounded to 2 children
The expected value is probably a mistake, since it is not a whole number of children
It is an average over many families, so it need not be a possible value
It means most families in the town have 1 or 2 children

items.q: A delivery takes 10, 20, 30 or 40 minutes with probabilities 0.2, 0.3, $p$ and 0.1. Find $p$, then find the mean delivery time in minutes.

mistakes.why: That averages 10, 20, 30 and 40 equally. Weight by the probabilities, with $p = 0.4$.
That leaves out the 40-minute term, $40(0.1) = 4$. Every value must be weighted and added.

items.q: For the tacos distribution, a student finds the mean as $\frac{1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5}{5} = 3$. What is wrong?

why.correct: Dividing by 5 treats the values as equally likely. Orders of 1 or 2 tacos are more likely than 4 or 5, so the probability-weighted mean is lower, 2.5.
options: Right: weight each value by its probability.
Dividing by the sum of the values gives 1, not a mean.
The middle of the list of values is not the mean of the distribution.
The mean is in tacos; it needs the values and the probabilities.
It ignores the probabilities, as if every order size were equally likely
It should divide by 15, the sum of the values
Nothing is wrong, since 3 is the middle value of the five order sizes
It should have used the probabilities alone, 0.2 on average

items.q: An insurance company sells a one-year policy for \$200. It pays \$5,000 if the insured item is stolen, which happens with probability 0.01. What is the company's expected profit per policy, in dollars?

why.correct: Profit is \$200 with probability 0.99 and \$200 − \$5,000 = −\$4,800 with probability 0.01: $\mu = 200(0.99) + (-4800)(0.01) = 198 - 48 = 150$ dollars per policy, on average over many policies.

mistakes.why: That is only $200(0.99)$. Add the theft case too: $(-4800)(0.01) = -48$.
That is the profit on a policy with a theft, not the long-run average.
